articles.title_orig: Inside the Ukrainian military unit training fighters from China
articles.title_zh: Inside the Ukrainian military unit training fighters from China
articles.content_orig:
Despite the risks, a number of soldiers from the country seen as Russia’s biggest backer have found their way to Ukraine
O n the makeshift workbench in the cramped front room of a cottage near the frontlines of the Russia-Ukraine war, there are all the accoutrements of a drone workshop . The walls are lined with pliers and rolls of duct tape; the table is cluttered with screwdrivers and piles of wire. Propped up against the wall are two kamikaze drones. Only one item looks out of place in this Ukrainian village house: a pot of Chinese longjing tea, the leaves wilted from repeated top-ups.
Good tea is one of the many things that Tim misses about his life in China. His parents post monthly supplies to Ukraine . “I think about all of it,” the 44-year-old said, of his home country. “It brings back memories and emotions.”
Tim’s teapot at the drone workshop
Tim, who asked to be referred to by his English name, is the lead volunteer in a Ukrainian military unit that this year launched an unusual project: to recruit soldiers from the country seen as Russia’s biggest backer, China .
Many Ukrainian military units have their own brands and public presences as they compete with each other for funding and new recruits. But in this case, the commander of the unit, which focuses on reconnaissance, asked that its identity be withheld because of the sensitivity of the Chinese volunteers project.
“It’s for their sake first and foremost,” said the commander, known by the call sign Muse. “For their own safety and that of their families.”
Muse said five Chinese men who had joined his unit had returned to China after completing their training because of pressure from the Chinese authorities. “We’d put our heart and soul into them,” he lamented. He is fearful that more Chinese soldiers – there are about a dozen so far in the unit – could quit if their identity is revealed. He asked that none of his soldiers’ faces be shown in photographs.
Ukraine’s military is facing an acute manpower shortage . Most of those willing to volunteer to fight have done so, and are fatigued, while some civilian men have gone into hiding to avoid being mobilised. That has turned attention to another pool of potential recruits: foreigners .
Memorial to Peng Chenliang, a Chinese soldier killed in action, fighting for Ukraine
Part of the memorial for fallen soldiers, dedicated to Chinese volunteers
There are about 16,000 foreign fighters in Ukraine, making up less than 3% of the armed forces. Before being sacked as defence minister in July, Mykhailo Fedorov passed several reforms designed to make foreign recruitment easier. He predicted that 50% of frontline service members or assault troops could be foreign citizens.
But Chinese volunteers present a unique challenge.
On the one hand, they are uniquely vulnerable to pressure from their own government. The Chinese authorities keep close tabs on their citizens. Chinese law does not specifically forbid citizens from joining foreign armies, but several Chinese volunteers in Ukraine said security services had questioned them or their relatives about their work.
A spokesperson for China’s foreign ministry said it had issued multiple security alerts “to ask Chinese nationals to stay away from areas of armed conflict … and, in particular, avoid participation in any party’s military operations”.
On the other hand, the Chinese soldiers hail from a country that has provided overwhelming support for Russia during the war in Ukraine. Although China claims to be neutral, Beijing has increased trade links with Moscow to record levels since 2022 and provided diplomatic support on numerous occasions. There have also been reports, denied by China, of high-level military cooperation between the two countries.
Roads covered with anti-drone nets in Sumy region
Some people worry that the Chinese soldiers in Ukraine could provide useful military intelligence to Beijing. An officer from another brigade said he would “think twice” before taking someone from China.
Muse, however, is unbothered. “In this situation, for us commanders, for the Ukrainian people, anyone will do. Because there aren’t enough people,” he said.
Tim, one of the Chinese volunteers, at his drone workshop
Plus, he added, the Chinese work hard. Tim’s main job in the unit is repairing drones. In one week he repaired about 10 Mavics and 15 first-person view (FPV) drones. Impressed, Muse joked that “it is better to have one Chinese person than 10 Ukrainians”.
Chinese volunteers find their way to Muse’s unit through social media and word of mouth. Although there are cursory background checks done by central authorities in Kyiv, Muse entrusts Tim to do the main screening, through a series of interviews.
Tim said the main qualities he looked for were a commitment to Ukraine’s democracy and sovereignty and an ability to communicate well. He added: “I am firmly against accepting someone who is driven simply by hatred for his own country.” He said he had already rejected more than 30 Chinese applicants since joining the unit himself in January, and that he attempted to screen out people with criminal records as well.
But in the murky world of foreign fighters, where people come with stories and claims that are often impossible to verify, dissatisfaction with one’s own country is often a factor.
Vanya, one of Chinese volunteer soldiers
Vanya, a 36-year-old from central China’s Hubei province, joined the unit over the summer.
Sitting under a trellis of grapevines outside a cottage near the frontlines, stalked by Russian FPV drones, he said life in China had become “suffocating”.
Using a VPN to jump over China’s firewall of internet censorship, he had read about the war in Ukraine, and become familiar with “ideas about democracy and freedom”. That awakening coincided with China’s own economic downturn . His own income, working in home renovations, fell by as much as 50% in some months.
He had long been interested in the military, but was too old to enlist in China. The decision to come to Ukraine “didn’t come out of the blue”, Vanya said. “It was the result of a lot of things building up over time: my weariness of my previous life, my longing for democracy and freedom, as well as my views on Ukraine.”
Nero, one of the Chinese volunteer soldiers
Other members of the unit claim a more fervent ideology. Nero, a 37-year-old from Fujian province, spent years posting online in support of Ukraine, becoming a well-known influencer. Several of his accounts were deleted; Nero thinks this was in response to his pro-Ukraine views.
He said the blowback he got from suspected Russian spam accounts for his support for Ukraine propelled him towards volunteering.
“I thought: the world shouldn’t be like this. Why should I suffer or go through all this just for speaking the truth?”
His move, which he publicised on social media, led to more harassment. As he arrived in Ukraine, a Russian-language “wanted” poster, which included his real name, date of birth, and picture, appeared online. The poster, which appeared to be faked, accused him of “participating in an armed conflict as a mercenary” and “illegally crossing the state border of the Russian federation”. Nero suspected it was produced by a Chinese propaganda agency working on behalf of Russia, and denied making it himself, saying that revealing his identity endangered him.
Until recently a project manager earning a decent salary in China, Nero is now training to be an FPV drone pilot. “I want people to know that not all Chinese people support Russia’s aggression. Many Chinese people, like me, are kind and want to help Ukraine,” Nero said.
L to R: Vasco, Nero, Jinmu, Chinese volunteer soldiers
All of the volunteers agreed that scrutiny from the Chinese authorities would make it difficult to return home. “If I go back now, it would be hard to leave again,” said Jinmu, a welder by trade, now working as an electrical engineer, specialising in explosives and batteries.

articles.title_orig: Ethiopia fighting escalates in Tigray killing 52 civilians in Alamata, medic tells the BBC
articles.title_zh: Ethiopia fighting escalates in Tigray killing 52 civilians in Alamata, medic tells the BBC
articles.content_orig:
At least 52 civilians have been killed during three days of heavy fighting around Alamata in Ethiopia's northern Tigray region, hospital sources have told the BBC.
It appears government troops have taken control of the town from regional fighters and intend to push north towards Mekelle, the region's main city. Social media clips show army tanks on Alamata's streets.
Clashes broke out last week after months of tension between the government and the party that controls Tigray, with both accusing each other of violating a 2022 deal that ended a two-year civil war.
Fighting has also affected neighbouring regions with 33 tourists stranded for the last week in Lalibela, a Unesco world heritage site.
"We have heard fighting, gunfire and artillery cannons firing throughout the week," a British tourist, who asked not to be named, told the BBC's Newsday programme about clashes near Lalibela in the Amhara region.
He said there was a large military presence in Lalibela, famous for being home to 13th Century churches hewn from rock and a holy site for millions of Orthodox Christians.
Most visitors to the tourist hub had been unable to leave since the airport closed to commercial flights last Wednesday, though he said 14 Israeli tourists had been evacuated by military helicopter on Monday.
The fighting around Lalibela has involved the army and an Amhara militia that has allied with Tigrayan fighters.
Earlier in September, they joined forces with other Ethiopian armed movements to form a seven-member alliance with the stated intention of removing the government in the capital, Addis Ababa.
There is also a fear that neighbouring Eritrea could be drawn into the conflict - as the government accuses Asmara of supporting the armed groups, something it  denies.
The BBC is unable to report from Tigray and surrounding areas and it is difficult to find out what is happening because communications to the region have been cut.
The two sides disagree over who started the latest fighting.
The Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), the party that runs Tigray, says it was responding to a federal offensive, including drone strikes, while the government says Tigrayan forces attacked first after seizing control of airports in the region.
TPLF fighters are also fighting in the Afar region, in a strategic area which connects landlocked Ethiopia to Djibouti and its ports.
Over the last few days, medical charity Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) said more than 700 wounded people had been admitted to hospitals it supports in Tigray.
The doctor at Alamata General Hospital, who requested anonymity, told the BBC the fighting in and around the town had taken place between Saturday and Monday, and involved heavy explosives and artillery, some of which landed in residential homes.
Those killed in the crossfire included children as young as three days old, mothers and cattle herders.
Twelve people had died in a single strike on the town's marketplace, the medic said.
Since the fighting erupted, banking services in Tigray have been suspended by the government. Access to the internet has also been cut - though it is not clear who ordered the closure.
A separate source in Alamata told the BBC there was a worsening humanitarian crisis in the area, as the town swelled with people fleeing fighting.
"All the residents of the surrounding areas entered the town of Alamata by walking on foot for as long as an hour, hoping the town would be safe.
"Unfortunately, everything is blocked - no banking service, no money transfer, no power, no internet, no phone. Hence people are in crisis, simply suffering, everyone is desperate and frustrated."
The British tourist in Lalibela said online banking was working in Lalibela but there was a shortage of physical cash.
He said the situation around the town had calmed down in the last two days and there were indications the airport, which was still being used by the military, might reopen on Thursday.
"The local people, they are still scared of what might happen. The military presence here in the town has remained and a larger military force has been seen leaving the town heading north," he said.
When the airport was first closed, 53 tourists had been in the town, he explained.
But some had since been evacuated, including the 14 Israelis airlifted out on Monday while another five had left the day before via an NGO convoy, despite advice not to travel by road.
Of the remaining tourists in Lalibela, the largest group were Americans, with Israelis, Britons, South Korean, South Africans, an Ethiopian-New Zealander and a Mexican also stranded, he said.
Meanwhile, for those cut off in Tigray because of the telecoms shutdown, the Tigray Broadcasting Service (TBS), based in Addis Ababa, has started an initiative to help reconnect families.
The broadcaster has said it will collect video messages via its Telegram channel from people outside the region and air them via satellite TV.
While limited to greetings and updates, this will provide a rare lifeline for families separated by the blackout.
The clampdown on Tigray's banking services is also affecting Tigrayans who are not physically in the region.
Customers have told the BBC that bank accounts opened in Tigray have been frozen or restricted.
"I boarded public transport from Addis Ababa to Adama and tried to pay using a mobile transfer, but it didn't work," said a former Mekelle resident who moved to the capital two months ago because of growing tensions in Tigray.
"It has created havoc for many people like me who escaped the situation in Tigray," he told the BBC's Tigrinya service.
"Many Tigrayans are now in trouble."

Apple ( AAPL ) stock rose in early trading on Wednesday following a report that the company is preparing to host an event next month outlining its entry into the smart home space.
According to Bloomberg's Mark Gurman , Apple will unveil an all-new smart home hub designed to control devices throughout the home, serve as a digital calendar and reminder list, play music, make video calls, and more.
Shares of Apple rose nearly 3%.
The hub, which can be mounted on a wall or placed on a counter with an accompanying stand, is designed to recognize users and provide them with personalized content via voice or facial recognition. It will also take advantage of Apple's new Siri AI platform, which it launched in beta earlier this month.
Apple is also working on a secondary version of the smart home hub featuring a robotic arm that lets the screen rotate 360 degrees.
The home hub would stand as the first new product category for Apple under CEO John Ternus , though the project has been in the works for some time. It could also serve as a lucrative new revenue stream for the company if it catches on.
Current do-it-yourself hub-style solutions require users to mount iPads to their walls to control smart home products or access them via their iPhones.
In addition to the hub, Apple is also rolling out new versions of its Apple TV set-top box and HomePod mini smart speaker. Both devices will look roughly the same as their existing versions, though they'll get more powerful processors to run Siri AI.
According to Gurman , Apple is looking to speed up its product development by making the company leaner via layoffs and other reductions.
Apple is entering a market traditionally dominated by Amazon ( AMZN ) and Google ( GOOG , GOOGL ), which had early success in the smart home space thanks to their Alexa and Google Assistant platforms, respectively.
The company's home offerings fall under its Wearables, Home, and Accessories segment, which brought in $35.68 billion in 2025, making it Apple's third-largest segment behind the iPhone and Services.
The iPhone, however, is still by far the company's most important product, bringing in $209.58 billion of Apple's $416.16 billion in total revenue last year.

articles.content_orig:

﻿What happens when platforms tell everyone how to optimize their content?
Instagram is the latest social media platform to add built-in AI-powered features that will give users feedback on their posts. The company announced Wednesday that its standalone Edits app will now include an AI “creative assistant” that pulls in data from a user’s Instagram account and offers suggestions on what to change.
Using the new assistant, creators can ask open-ended questions about what’s trending on Instagram, why one video worked and another didn’t, or what piece of content resonated most with their audience. The tool pulls in data and metrics such as likes, views, retention on videos, and shares. Instagram says it can spot patterns over time and give a creator suggestions that metrics alone can’t provide. Creators can also ask for ideas for content, how to hook viewers, what captions to use, which audio tracks are trending, and how to script videos.
I want to hear from you about your experience. Contact me at mia@theverge.com or at miasato.11 on Signal.
If that sounds familiar, it’s because YouTube also just announced updates to its sprawling AI-powered dashboard that tells creators how to maximize engagement. (YouTube’s version, which it initially announced in 2025, also has AI editing and A/B testing capabilities.) If you’ve been online for a while — and especially if you’ve ever had to pay attention to social media metrics — you’ll know that this is quite a shift. Historically, many platforms have limited or even hidden detailed metrics about how your own content is performing. The platforms certainly have not been open about why a video or post performed poorly. Tools like CrowdTangle, which researchers and journalists used to monitor the most popular content on Meta platforms , have been shut down or restricted . Now, both YouTube and Instagram are effectively promising to give creators personalized advice on how to ride the algorithm.
It’s in both the platforms’ and creators’ best interest to shape content for maximum engagement. As I wrote earlier this month , though, what happens when everyone is perfectly optimizing their content? Will content become even more similar as creators adjust to one another? Is there no ceiling for the amount of time audiences are willing to spend on the platforms? The shift also raises interesting new questions about the relationship between tech companies and the creators that fill the platforms with things to look at: How does this dynamic change when platforms are straightforwardly giving creators instructions on how to post?
The new feature is free for creators to use, up to a point. Meta says “power users” will be able to buy a Meta One subscription for more usage. This, too, speaks to the changing winds: Meta needs to finance its lofty AI ambitions , and it’s already signaled that premium social media features may be part of how it does it. It’s not hard to imagine a future where meaningful feedback and AI-driven analytics and insights are for paying subscribers. In the end, it may end up re-creating the same frustrations and opaqueness that have plagued content creators for years — but this time, behind a paywall.

articles.title_orig: DA in Cornell University case says he never saw transcript of campus police interview with alleged rape victim
articles.title_zh: DA in Cornell University case says he never saw transcript of campus police interview with alleged rape victim
articles.content_orig:
Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten says he never saw a transcript of a conversation between an alleged rape victim and investigators showing what she told Cornell University campus police before his office decided not to bring charges.
The transcript , which CBS News New York exclusively obtained from a source, shows the victim told campus police more than three weeks after the alleged assault,  "I can say with 100% confidence I was raped."
"I'm going to follow up on this because this is news to me," Van Houten told CBS News New York on Tuesday about the transcript .
Cornell conducted an internal investigation into the alleged fraternity gang rape that occurred Oct. 19-20, 2024, and led to expulsions, suspensions and other sanctions. Criminal charges, however, were not pursued, and prosecutors have now reopened their criminal investigation as the law enforcement response has come under new scrutiny.
Van Houten said his decision not to bring charges was based on the contents of a 2024 statement signed by Jane Doe, the alleged victim.
When Van Houten was told by CBS News New York's Mahsa Saeidi that Jane Doe had said she was confident she was raped, Van Houten said, "That wasn't information that I had, first of all. Second of all, that is a legal conclusion."
"If she had said those words, we certainly would want to have explored that more," Van Houten continued. "Like I said, that wasn't provided to me."
The DA said he'd seek the transcript and follow up with Cornell Police.
"Nobody knows this information about the transcript and that gives me something to really dig into because that changes the landscape for me," Van Houten said.
Cornell University said its police department provided the results of the school's investigation to the DA.
Jane Doe's interview, as seen in the transcript, began on Nov. 14 — more than three weeks after the alleged gang rape — and continued the next day. A campus police investigator led the questioning. A Title IX investigator, a victim advocate, and Jane Doe's adviser were also in the room for the first day of the interview.
According to the transcript, Jane Doe described drinking and using drugs the night of the alleged rape, and said she had gaps in her memory.
The transcript shows she distinguished the initial sexual activity from what she says happened later, and when asked whether she was OK with the initial encounter, she said, "Yeah, as much as I can be because, again, I was super drunk when I got there ... But I was pretty OK with all of this."
Jane Doe added, according to the transcript, "And then, of course, I was being hit at the same time. Physically hit very, very hard."
According to the transcript, she said she didn't remember the end of the night "where I was raped" and didn't know how many people had sex with her.
When describing what happened later in the night, the transcript says Jane Doe said, "I can say with 100% confidence I was raped."
The transcript shows that throughout the interview, the investigator asks questions as he prepares her written statement.
Before discussing what Jane Doe said when men asked her for sex, the transcript says the investigator warned her that his questions may sound accusatory, but said he needed specific answers to determine the right charges.
According to the transcript, Jane Doe said she swatted one man's hand away and told him she was uncomfortable, and she told another man no a few times or that she was too tired.
"Was it 'no' or was it, 'eh, I'm tired'?" the investigator asked, according to the transcript.
The transcript says Jane Doe responded, "I think it's 'I'm tired.'"
According to the transcript, the investigator later asked whether she got tired of answering the men's questions asking for sex, and gave in.
"Yes. It was coercion, yes," Jane Doe said, according to the transcript. She also said she was "completely and totally incapacitated."
The transcript shows the investigator documenting her account, reading it back and asking her to clarify or correct it.
On the second day of the interview, Jane Doe reviewed the revised six-page statement. The transcript shows her adviser asked if she wanted her and another adviser to review the statement.
Before signing, the transcript shows Jane Doe said, "I'm very confident about this."
Jane Doe's attorney, Thomas Giuffra, told CBS News, "What more did (Van Houten) need to do a thorough investigation and prosecute? He had a woman who told an officer she was raped and a group chat inviting sexual assaults. The failure to do anything is shocking."
"Neither I nor Ms. Doe have any confidence in DA Houten's ability to handle this investigation and prosecution," Giuffra said. "He seems more interested in protecting his reputation as opposed to seeking justice as is his duty as the District Attorney."
Previously, Giuffra said his client was in denial after the alleged attack.
CBS News New York has not seen Jane Doe's final six-page statement. CBS News New York reached out to Cornell and has not heard back.
CBS News New York is in touch with attorneys for two defendants named in the lawsuit, and they say their clients deny the charges.

articles.title_zh: Vikings Insiders Dish on 'Brutal' J.J. McCarthy Era, 'Eye-Rolls' About 'Nine' Nickname
articles.content_orig:
It sounds like the Minnesota Vikings won't be looking back fondly at the J.J. McCarthy era after this week's trade with the New York Giants.
The Athletic's Alec Lewis spoke to a team staffer who revealed that the Vikings had lost faith in McCarthy since his disappointing 2025 season.
"I knew this was going to be up and down when we made that choice this spring (to move forward with McCarthy as the starter), but it has just been brutal," the staffer said.
The Vikings moved up in the 2024 NFL draft to select McCarthy 10th overall. His shortcomings were quickly on display, as Lewis reported that "in the immediate aftermath of the draft, several team sources acknowledged that McCarthy had work to do. He would have to eliminate his overstriding on throws and develop better touch."
After missing his entire rookie year due to knee surgery, McCarthy was handed the reins as Minnesota's starting quarterback entering the 2025 campaign. However, he struggled to stay healthy and appeared in just 10 games due to multiple injuries, finishing with 1,632 yards, 11 touchdowns and 12 interceptions. The Vikings brought in veteran signal-caller Kyler Murray this offseason, and McCarthy was demoted to QB3 behind him and veteran backup Carson Wentz.
Lewis also explained that McCarthy's immaturity affected his tenure in Minnesota. His comments regarding his "Nine" alter ego reportedly "earned several internal eye-rolls," and he "similarly baffled members of the organization when he told reporters that he bucked his coaches' advice by dancing the 'Griddy' before he reached the end zone against the Cowboys in Week 15."
"These bouts of youth and defiance, evident both in front of the cameras and away from them inside the TCO Performance Center, were troubling for Vikings executives and coaches," Lewis added.
Now, McCarthy will have to win over a new franchise as he makes a fresh start with the Giants, who acquired him after second-year quarterback Jaxson Dart suffered a season-ending knee injury. He will serve as the backup to veteran signal-caller Jameis Winston, so he should use the rest of the 2026 season to learn and develop as he tries to revive his reputation.

Riz Ahmed was getting ready for his big confrontation with Tom Cruise . The two actors were playing a scientist and a hell-catting oilman in “ Digger ,” who face off in a swanky private jet over an ecological disaster triggered by humanity’s relentless pursuit of black gold. It was January 2025, and just as cameras were about to roll, news broke that a raging forest fire was threatening large swaths of Los Angeles.
“I remember looking out at the crew who were watching the fire move in real time through satellite imagery, and they were thinking, ‘I’m about to lose my home,'” Ahmed said. “It was right there. So much of what is explored, exposed, and satirized in this film was staring us right in the face.”
“Digger,” which opens on Friday, has been in the works for nearly a decade. The absurdist look at greed and climate change, reality and the distorting power of media, feckless world leaders and rapacious billionaires, struggled to get off the ground. Alejandro G. Iñárritu, its co-writer and director, said the production collapsed three times during a period that saw Hollywood battered by COVID and labor strikes before Warner Bros. and Legendary took a leap of faith and backed the movie to the tune of $125 million.
“In the world of fear we are living in, everybody wants certainty,” Iñárritu said over Zoom a few hours before “Digger’s” Los Angeles premiere. “This film is not any of that. For it to be made and to nail the tone was a big bet. But to their credit, Warner Bros. and Legendary were really bold. They never hesitated. They believed in this film — the urgency, the absurdity, the humanity, the nowness that it has.”
As he labored to get “Digger” made, Iñárritu began to feel like events were overtaking his story. As shooting happened, Donald Trump returned to office, reintroducing his reality TV show approach to government, and Elon Musk took a literal chainsaw to the federal workforce. In the lead-up to “Digger’s” release, various AI executives and tech moguls have warned about the technology’s destructive power . The lines between Iñárritu’s fiction and our demented present are clearly blurring.
“We are living in a satire,” Iñárritu said. “The more we stretched our imagination, reality was chasing and catching us. It was crazy. Now I think the tone of the film feels almost realistic because if you turn on the TV, this is what is going on. The people in power are trying to convince all of us that everything is fine, and people want to buy that, and that’s the power of someone like Digger.”
Initially, the film wasn’t named for Cruise’s character, Digger Rockwell. It was intended to be entitled “Blah, Blah, Blah.”
“It was a reference to this incredible, terrible, terrifying weapon that we as humans have, which is the tongue,” Iñárritu said. “It can change your perception of the reality that your body is experiencing. It can make you believe in something that you don’t see.”
One thing you don’t see often is Cruise abandoning vanity to play a potbellied mogul with a thick Texas drawl and thinning hair. The physical transformation originally took six hours (Cruise challenged the makeup team to get it down to one ), but it was a change that the movie star embraced with abandon.
“He’s so handsome,” Iñárritu said. “He looks like he’s 40 years old. There’s no white man with that look. Nobody will believe it. He’s not someone off of Wall Street. He’s from the South of the United States … But I think he loved it because it liberated him to be playful, to suddenly get into the skin of another person that is not Tom Cruise, and he nailed it.”
Ahmed shares several pivotal moments with Cruise, including a drunken clash just as Digger is about to address a collection of world leaders about the environmental disaster he unleashed. The “Sound of Metal” Oscar nominee praised his co-star as a scene partner.
“Tom is meticulous — he has the precision of a stuntman,” Ahmed said. “His spatial awareness, his sense of movement, his physicality is something he’s so in command of. And his awareness of the camera and of the frame informs his behavior in this way that is very intuitive. It’s wondrous to watch.”
And Cruise often served as a cheerleader for the rest of the cast.
“Once in rehearsal, I did something, and it clearly didn’t work, and we were about to move on,” Ahmed remembered. “But before we did, Tom stopped the rehearsal and gave me a round of applause to say, ‘Well done for trying something.’ He wanted us to take big swings because this film is such a big swing.”
In addition to being one of the year’s biggest commercial risks — a savage and surreal social satire produced on the scale of a studio blockbuster — “Digger” is nearly impossible to discuss without spoiling it. About a third of the way through, a moment completely reorients the story and sends it in a direction that is, well, Brechtian (bet you can’t say that about “Days of Thunder 2”). Both Iñárritu and Ahmed confess they’re having a tough time dancing around the big reveal.
“I want to make sure people are surprised when they see the film,” Iñárritu said. “It’s difficult. That’s why our trailers were like, ‘What is this about?’ Well, we cannot say anything more.”
It was a twist that  Iñárritu said he came up with years into “Digger’s” development.
“I was on a hiking holiday with my young daughter, and I was just thinking, ‘How are we going to tell this story?'” Iñárritu said. “And as I was strolling, I realized that the only way to tell this story is by being separated from it in some way. That separation will allow us to recognize ourselves without killing each other.”
“Digger” offers a warning about the perilous course humanity is taking, but Iñárritu wasn’t interested in offering up a screed. He paid particular attention to a 10-minute speech Digger Rockwell delivers to a room full of presidents, prime ministers, and ambassadors, in which he acknowledges both the terrible consequences of our relentless pursuit of oil and the creature comforts it provides. Are we really prepared to make a sacrifice for the greater good?
“I’m not interested in pointing fingers or reducing the film to a political commentary or a right or left thing,” Iñárritu said. “I’m trying, through Digger’s speech, to say that we are all part of this madness. That there are no good people or bad people. The system has trapped all of us, and we have to find a way out together.”
“Digger” opens in theaters on October 2 from Warner Bros. Pictures .
